# 2 Kings Chapter 12 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 233r–233v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2KI_012_page_001.jpg, 2KI_012_page_002.jpg

---

**1** Joash became king in the seventh year of Jehu's reign and ruled in Jerusalem for forty years. His mother was Zibiah from Beersheba.

**2** Joash did what was right in the LORD's eyes throughout the years that Jehoiada the priest guided him.

**3** The high places, however, were not torn down. The people continued to offer sacrifices and burn incense there.

**4** Joash told the priests, "Collect all the money brought as sacred offerings to the LORD's temple — the census money, personal assessment fees, and all voluntary contributions.

**5** Each priest should collect from his own contacts, and use it to repair whatever damage is found in the temple."

**6** But by the twenty-third year of Joash's reign, the priests still had not made any repairs.

**7** So King Joash called in Jehoiada and the other priests and demanded, "Why haven't you repaired the temple? From now on, stop collecting money from your contacts. Hand it all over for temple repairs."

**8** The priests agreed: they would no longer collect money from the people, and they would no longer be responsible for repairs.

**9** Jehoiada the priest came up with a solution. He took a chest, bored a hole in the lid, and placed it next to the altar on the right side as people entered the LORD's temple. The priests who guarded the entrance deposited all the money into it.

**10** Whenever the chest was full, the king's secretary and the high priest would come, bag the money, and count it.

**11** Then they handed the counted silver over to the foremen supervising the temple project. These foremen paid the carpenters and builders working on the LORD's temple,

**12** as well as the masons and stonecutters. They also purchased timber and cut stone — covering every expense needed to restore the temple.

**13** None of the money was used to make silver basins, wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, trumpets, or any gold or silver articles for the temple.

**14** It all went directly to the workers doing the repairs.

**15** No one audited the men who distributed the money to the workers, because they were completely trustworthy.

**16** Money from guilt offerings and sin offerings did not go into the temple fund — that money belonged to the priests.

**17** Around this time, King Hazael of Aram marched against Gath and captured it. Then he turned his attention toward Jerusalem.

**18** Joash king of Judah gathered up all the sacred objects that his ancestors Jehoshaphat, Joram, and Ahaziah had dedicated, along with his own offerings and all the gold in the treasuries of the temple and the palace, and sent everything to Hazael. The Aramean king withdrew.

**19** The rest of Joash's reign — everything he accomplished — is recorded in the court history of the kings of Judah.

**20** His own officials conspired against him and assassinated him at Beth-millo, on the road going down to Silla.

**21** The assassins were Jozachar son of Shimeath and Jehozabad son of Shomer — trusted servants who struck him down. He was buried with his ancestors in the City of David, and his son Amaziah succeeded him.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 2 — "all the days in which Jehoiada instructed him":** A loaded qualifier. Joash does right only while his priestly mentor lives. The narrator is already foreshadowing trouble — this king's righteousness is borrowed, not internalized.

**Verse 6 — Twenty-three years of inaction:** The priests collected money for two decades but made no repairs. This is institutional corruption hidden behind religious authority — the kind of systemic failure that requires structural reform, not just moral appeals.

**Verse 9 — The collection box:** Jehoiada's chest is a stroke of administrative genius. By centralizing donations and making them visible (beside the altar, where everyone passes), he removes the priests as middlemen and creates accountability. It is one of the earliest recorded examples of institutional financial reform.

**Verse 15 — "completely trustworthy":** In a chapter about institutional failure (the priests' misuse of funds) and national failure (buying off Hazael), this statement about faithful workers shines. Integrity exists at the individual level even when institutions crumble.

**Verse 18 — The tragic arc:** The same king who restored the temple now empties it to buy off an enemy. The chapter's structure tells the story: build (vv.4–16), then lose everything (vv.17–18), then die by conspiracy (vv.20–21). Joash's legacy is ultimately one of promise unfulfilled.

*— PNEUMA*
